utterances.text: Your Honour, all matters that the Prosecutor was obliged to disclose to the accused have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must say straight away that before I arrived at court today, it was quite clear to me that it is not possible to raise any legal matters linked to these documents, and I really had no intention to go into any matters of law in that connection. When I tried to rise at the beginning, I simply wanted to point out that Mr. Nice, at one point in time, did indeed say that the Prosecution was impartial, because in the document tab 9 there is reference to the suffering of the Serbs. These were the words uttered by Mr. Nice, and I simply wanted to say that and nothing more. So my questions will be very brief, and I will deal only with the document under tab 11. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a letter sent to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic on the 26th of March of 1999. Mr. Blewitt, on the 26th of March when this letter was sent, wasn't that two days after the beginning of the NATO bombing campaign in Kosovo or, rather, after the beginning of the war which went on for a couple of months? Wasn't that two days after the beginning of the war, because the war started on the 24th?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: I think, in answer to an earlier question, I indicated I couldn't recall the date of the commencement of the NATO bombing, however I was prepared to accept the proposition that it commenced on the 24th of March, and I still adhere to that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since Ms. Arbour, and I'm sorry that she's not present because she might be able to answer this better, but in this letter as quoted by Mr. Nice, it is stated that a request was made to investigate all serious violations of international humanitarian law, on the 26th of March. Can you answer this question: Was it possible under conditions of war, during a bombing campaign when all of those people were in jeopardy, was it possible to ensure investigations until the war ended, that is, sometime in June? So was it possible to respond adequately to a request of this kind at that time and under those conditions?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I'm in a position to answer that question. However, this letter was a culmination of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let the witness finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This letter dated the 26th of March, 1999, was a culmination of a series of attempts by the Prosecutor and the Prosecutor's office to investigate the crimes that had been allegedly committed in Kosovo since the beginning of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we also refer to what is stated in the first paragraph of this letter when there is mention of the departure of the Kosovo Verification Mission, which meant that the presence of independent observers has been severely curtailed. Mr. Slobodan Milosevic is not charged with any crimes in 1998 but mostly for acts in 1999. That is, up until March, the Verification Mission was there. For example, Racak, it was investigated by the Verification Mission. And the Verification Mission was present in Kosovo and was able to monitor events. It was not prevented from investigating any such things. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: I believe that to be the case; correct. However, the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: However, the Prosecutor's office had been prevented from undertaking on-site investigations in Kosovo since the latter part of 1998, and it was the Prosecutor who is mandated by the Security Council to investigate matters falling within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, not the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree, but the Verification Mission came there with the permission of the state in which it was working, and the Verification Mission did conduct investigations in certain cases, and this was done in accordance with the authority granted by the authorities in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: I certainly do not dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, please. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Blewitt, go to tab 9, the report, and go to paragraph 36 on page 26. It's a passage we've looked at before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher would be good enough to just put it on the table or the overhead projector if we can find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want you to look at this paragraph given the questions you've been asked about the use of the term "terrorism" and the suggestion that there was in some way a biased approach, taking account not of the Kosovo Albanian crimes, if any, committed. This passage reads, I remind us, as follows: "The Prosecutor concluded that the information was credible and tended to show that crimes within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal may have been committed in Kosovo. In particular, the Prosecutor concluded that credible information tends to show that an armed conflict may exist in Kosovo, and that fighting was and is going on between two sides: military and police forces connected to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and/or the Republic of Serbia on one hand, and armed and organised units and groups, including the KLA, associated with the Kosovar Albanian community on the other." Now, does that passage and that sentence reflect an approach at the time of this letter to both sides of what was thought to be an internal conflict?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused has been pressing you to adopt the term "terrorism," which you've declined to do. "Armed and organised units and groups associated with the KLA and the Kosovar Albanian community," does that reflect the approach that the office was taking to actions by the Kosovo Albanians at that time?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, totally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say: "The level and intensity of violence used by the armed groups involved may be illustrated by the resort to the armed forces by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but also by the devastating impact on the civilian population, and is further evidenced by the involvement of the international community. This all tends to show that an armed conflict may be going on in Kosovo, giving rise to violence which may constitute crimes within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal." Now, does that passage refer only to one wrongdoer or does it countenance the possibility of wrongdoing on both sides?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: I think it clearly indicates that there was an armed conflict involving two parties to that conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've spoken both briefly here but more particularly through the letters that you've produced, of the restrictions on access imposed on the OTP in 1998, 1999. Did those restrictions impede investigations into just one side of any wrongdoing or into both sides?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: Clearly they impeded the investigations into all parties to the conflict and both sides identified in the report that you've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally on this topic, and I think my last question for you, as a matter of fact and history, does the Office of the Prosecutor investigate crimes alleged to have been committed by the other side, by the KLA, by Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: It does indeed, and in fact there is still an ongoing investigation into crimes allegedly committed by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And process in respect of another indictment has already been undertaken?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No other questions -- oh, one other question, yes. The accused asked you a question that didn't go very far about the independence of the Prosecution from the rest of the Tribunal. With that question in mind, can you have tab 7 in mind, which is the letter from the then-president, Gabrielle Kirk McDonald, to the president of the Security Council, and it's clear that that letter incorporates complaints coming from the OTP. Can you just explain how it is necessary and how to comes about that the president of the Tribunal has to record complaints of the OTP in these particular circumstances.

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: In the event of lack of cooperation on the part of a state, or a state not fulfilling its legal obligations towards the Tribunal as required as a consequence of the Security Council resolution, the only mechanism that the Tribunal can take in that regard is to report the matter to the Security Council, and under the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, it is only the president of this Tribunal that is empowered and authorised to make such a report to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to that extent it's necessary for the OTP to report to the president for the president to report onwards to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: GRAHAM BLEWITT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other questions of the witness, but, Your Honour, may I, before he leaves the witness box in case there should be anything the Chamber would want to ask of him arising from this, may I remind the Chamber, but in reality perhaps remind the accused through the Chamber, of the following given his question about Rule 68 provision and NATO bombing. Two points: One, provision of a considerable amount of material judged to be potentially Rule 68 has been provided to him and has indeed been referred to by him, as I recall, in the Kosovo section of this case. And the second point that he might not have in mind and remember is that at all times we have been at pains to reveal how we're dealing with the provision of exculpatory material to the accused. We have invited him and his associates to take part in the discussions about those arrangements so he can be satisfied he is receiving exactly what he should receive, and he has at all times declined to take part in those arrangements. I have no other questions of Mr. Blewitt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Blewitt, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there were various administrative matters to deal with, and I have in mind in particular the finalisation of the witness list and also the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness list in final version was provided to you on the 21st of October of this year, Trafalgar Day, as it happens to be. There was one name omitted from the list by oversight, and you'll receive notification of that in due course, but the list is otherwise complete. To call the witnesses on that list would require the granting of leave to add a certain number of witnesses. The application to add those witnesses, an omnibus document, was a document I hoped to serve on you yesterday. In the event, there were one or two queries about protective measures that were not complete yesterday, I think can be completed today, so the document will be with you today. For reasons explained in the document, it cannot deal with absolutely all those witnesses whom we apply to add to the list but very nearly all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the matter of concern is that here we are, nearly two years into the Prosecution case, and the list is not finalised. Now, for whatever reasons, and I accept they may be beyond the control of the Prosecutor, there comes a time when the accused is entitled to know who the witnesses are against him, and also the Trial Chamber, and the idea that there are yet further applications coming is a matter of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the application that will be with you today simply is the necessary application to reflect the names on the list served on the 21st of October. The names in the list on the 21st of October are, for the most part, names or identities made known to the Chamber and to the accused and the amici over the last several months where we've noted that it was our intention to call particular people, whether named or not, and that applications would be forthcoming in a compendious way rather than piecemeal. I can give in the most general terms the reasons for the lateness of -- for the timing of applications for many of these witnesses. There are categories of witnesses -- sorry. There is a category of witnesses who have been subject to Rule 70 restrictions that it has taken a very great deal of time to deal with outside our control. There are witnesses who have only very recently come to light, and if they are in a position to offer very valuable evidence, then it's obviously our duty to seek to add them. And I think that's probably the two most important categories. But, Your Honour, for the most part, all parties have been on notice for most of these witnesses for some time that an application would be forthcoming, and it is our submission that there is no prejudice suffered by the list being formulated on the 21st of October and the application coming, as it will, this afternoon. But obviously the Chamber will have to consider the application which deals with witnesses on an item-by-item basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So can I take it that this compendious application will be the last that we will receive on this topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For reasons that -- there are a couple of witnesses who just simply can't be named for reasons outside our control, and it's explained that they will have to come later, but that is the position subject to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a question of how much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Days. I hope not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's matter of days, obviously then that's something we can consider, but more would be a difficulty, because we are coming to the end of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand that. May I make the point that sense the first publication of this effectively final list, which obviously has been final but changing, we have been as transparent as we possibly can about our approach to witnesses. As the Court will know, we have regularly been dropping witnesses in large numbers in order to meet the timetable requirements and to reflect the expressed views of the Trial Chamber about the amount of evidence of crime base, as it's called, that may be required, and so on, and I would respectfully suggest that the transparency of this document, which is a document I hope that becomes familiar to the Trial Chamber and to its officers and enables them to see at a glance how things are developing, how witnesses are being withdrawn to save time, how witness difficulties are being resolved, I would hope that this document may in fact serve as a model for other cases because it provides a transparency that is appropriate to this type of process. This is not the sort of trial where, in my judgement, it is necessary for the Prosecution to keep things close to their chest. It's the sort of case where the maximum possible disclosure is desirable and in everybody's interests, and that's what we've done. The list, of course, also has that the ready reckoner advantage where we record the time we expect witnesses to take and we, after the event, are able to adjust to reflect the amount of time that witnesses have taken and in that way to see the degree to which we are going to be able to fit witnesses into the remaining time or not, that imposing on us, of course, the necessity of making further adjustments. So it's quite a useful document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Turning to exhibits, we have in mind issuing an order for a finalisation of the exhibit list so that not only the accused but also the Trial Chamber may be satisfied that we have a final list. We propose to do that in 21 days -- or give you, rather, 21 days to produce your definitive list. Is there any reason why you should not be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not alive to any at the moment, and I have to say I think that seems a sensible course to take. If I find any reason why -- to resist that, I'll perhaps come back to you, but I very much hope not to. I've been concerned not only that the prospective exhibit list should be clarified but we should take steps now with your legal officer and Registry to ensure there is absolute certainty about the state of exhibits tendered to date. I can remember on other cases where that's proved to be quite a major exercise to conduct at the end of the Prosecution's case, or at the end of the case overall. I'm alive to the fact that there are a number of exhibits that have been tendered without being produced. In the case of some of those exhibits, resolution of the status of the exhibit may be capable -- may be susceptible to argument; in other cases it may simply be that the exhibit won't be produced or won't be produced unless we produce further evidence. For example, the intercepts are a case in point. So I'm very concerned that we may be able to get together, the various parties, and ensure that that part of the documentation is as clear as it can be before the close of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The individual exhibits should be clarified as to their position.
